limits: The authors state that linearity is a working model: 'we seldom believe that the true relationship is linear' (footnote 1, p73).
Standard errors, CIs and tests assume uncorrelated errors with constant variance; the authors say this is clearly untrue for the TV fit in Fig 3.1 but the formulas remain a good approximation.
The +/- 2 SE interval is approximate; exact intervals use the 97.5% t quantile with n-2 df and assume Gaussian errors (footnote 3).
The F test and least squares fail when p > n; the chapter defers high-dimensional methods to Chapter 6 and multiple testing to Chapter 13.
R2, RSE and the VIF discussion are training-set measures; the chapter says R2 always rises with added variables and that test error is the real target.
Only classical subset selection (forward, backward, mixed) is outlined; Mallow's Cp, AIC, BIC and adjusted R2 are named but deferred to Chapter 6.
Chapter gives no sample size for the Credit and Auto data sets, and the exercises have no answers.
Text swaps the signs of the South and West region coefficients against Table 3.8 (see results note).
practices: Plot residuals against fitted values (or the predictor) to detect non-linearity, and look for a U shape (Sec 3.3.3, Fig 3.9, p100-101).
If residuals show non-linearity, try log X, sqrt X or X squared, or polynomial terms, which remain linear models (Sec 3.3.2-3.3.3, p98, 101).
Plot residuals against time or order to detect tracking from correlated errors, and rely on good experimental design to prevent them (Sec 3.3.3, p101-102).

For a funnel-shaped residual plot, transform the response with a concave function such as log Y or sqrt Y, or use weighted least squares with weights proportional to inverse variance (Sec 3.3.3, p103).
Use studentized residuals and flag |value| > 3 as possible outliers; remove a point only when it is a recording error, since it may signal a missing predictor (Sec 3.3.3, p104).
Compute leverage h_i and compare it with (p+1)/n; examine points that have both high leverage and a large studentized residual (Sec 3.3.3, p105-106).
Detect collinearity with VIF rather than only the correlation matrix, treating VIF above 5 or 10 as a problem; fix it by dropping a variable or combining standardised variables (Sec 3.3.3, p108-109).
Test the overall F-statistic before reading individual p-values, since with p = 100 null predictors about 5 will show p < 0.05 by chance (Sec 3.2.2, p86).
Use a prediction interval for an individual response and a confidence interval for an average response; the prediction interval is always wider (Sec 3.2.2, 3.4, p90, 110).
Follow the hierarchical principle: keep main effects when their interaction is in the model, even if the main effects have large p-values (Sec 3.3.2, p96-97).
With more than two levels use one fewer dummy variable than levels, and test the factor with an F-test because coefficient p-values depend on the baseline chosen (Sec 3.3.1, p93-94).
Use forward, backward or mixed selection when 2^p subsets are too many; backward selection cannot be used if p > n (Sec 3.2.2, p87).
Prefer linear regression to KNN when there are few observations per predictor, when the truth is near linear, or when interpretability matters (Sec 3.5, p115).

terms.definition: an estimate of the standard deviation of epsilon; RSE = sqrt(RSS/(n - p - 1)), in the units of Y
R2 = (TSS - RSS)/TSS, the proportion of variability in Y explained by the regression; equals the squared correlation of Y with fitted Y
F = ((TSS - RSS)/p) / (RSS/(n - p - 1)), tests H0 that all slope coefficients are zero; near 1 under H0
the association between X1 and Y depends on X2; modelled by adding the product X1 X2
if an interaction is included, the main effects should be included too, even if their p-values are not significant
a confidence interval covers average response f(X); a prediction interval covers an individual Y and is wider because it adds the irreducible error
non-constant variance of error terms, shown by a funnel shape in the residual plot
each residual divided by its estimated standard error; |value| > 3 suggests an outlier
h_i = 1/n + (x_i - xbar)^2 / sum (x_i' - xbar)^2 in simple regression; in [1/n, 1] with mean (p+1)/n
ratio of the variance of beta_j_hat in the full model to its variance fit alone, 1/(1 - R2 of Xj onto the other predictors)
indicator variable for a level of a factor; one fewer than the number of levels, the omitted level being the baseline
f_hat(x0) is the average of the training responses of the K observations closest to x0
in high dimensions the K nearest neighbors of a point may be very far away, so KNN predictions degrade
forward selection that removes any variable whose p-value rises above a threshold

figures.caption: For the Advertising data, the least squares fit for the regression of sales onto TV is shown. The fit is found by minimizing the residual sum of squares. Each grey line segment represents a residual.
figures.why: Shows residuals as vertical segments, the picture of what RSS minimises.

figures.caption: A simulated data set. Left: population regression line f(X)=2+3X and the least squares line. Right: ten least squares lines from ten data sets.
figures.why: Shows sampling variability of OLS lines around the population line, i.e. what unbiased and standard error mean.

figures.caption: For the Advertising data, a linear regression fit to sales using TV and radio as predictors. From the pattern of the residuals, we can see that there is a pronounced non-linear relationship in the data.
figures.why: Motivates the interaction term: residual pattern shows the synergy.

figures.caption: For the Credit data, least squares lines for prediction of balance from income for students and non-students. Left: no interaction. Right: with interaction.
figures.why: Parallel lines versus different slopes explains a dummy x quantitative interaction.

figures.caption: The Auto data set. mpg and horsepower; linear (orange), degree 2 (blue), degree 5 (green) fits.
figures.why: Underfit, good fit and wiggly fit for polynomial regression in one plot.

figures.caption: Residuals versus fitted values for the Auto data. Left: linear fit shows a U shape. Right: quadratic fit shows little pattern.
Residuals from simulated time series with adjacent-error correlation rho = 0.0, 0.5, 0.9.
figures.why: Shows what tracking looks like as error correlation rises.

figures.caption: Residual plots. Left: funnel shape indicates heteroscedasticity. Right: response log transformed.
figures.why: Funnel shape and the log-transform fix.

figures.caption: Left: observation 41 is a high leverage point, while 20 is not. Center: a point unusual only jointly. Right: studentized residual versus leverage.
figures.why: Separates outlier from leverage and shows the leverage versus studentized-residual plot.

figures.caption: Contour plots of RSS as a function of beta for Credit regressions. Left: balance on age and limit. Right: balance on rating and limit, narrow valley from collinearity.
figures.why: Geometric picture of why collinearity makes coefficients unstable.

figures.caption: KNN versus least squares test MSE with slightly and strongly non-linear truths, as a function of 1/K.
figures.why: Shows when non-parametric beats parametric as non-linearity grows.

figures.caption: Test MSE for linear regression and KNN as the number of noise variables p increases from 1 to 20.
figures.why: Direct demonstration of the curse of dimensionality for KNN.
